newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. to prepare statement on Iraq copter incidents.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to prepare statement on Iraq copter incidents.

text.p: Security Council members decided on Wednesday to draft a presidential statement criticising alleged Iraqi interference with U.N. helicopters working with weapons inspection teams, council members said.
The decision followed a briefing by Rolf Ekeus, head of the U.N. special commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction.

In a letter on Tuesday to council President Sergei Lavrov of Russia, Ekeus said there had been "four serious incidents" last week in which Iraqi personnel aboard the U.N. helicopters, or Iraqi helicopters flying nearby, had endangered the U.N. craft and their crews.

In an incident on June 4, he said, an Iraqi shut off the fuel pump of a U.N. helicopter and manhandled the chief air inspector and UNSCOM's photographer to prevent them from taking photographs of an inspection site, including the departure from the site of two Iraqi helicopters.

The U.N. flights are to ensure that nothing is removed surreptitiously from sites being inspected by U.N. ground teams. Iraq has challenged the U.N. account of the incidents and said the helicopters were flying over "sensitive" areas.

Chile, which is a Security Council member and has provided five helicopters and about 40 crew members for UNSCOM in Iraq, was said to be taking the lead in drafting a statement. The text is to be discussed by council members in closed-door consultations on Thursday.

Meanwhile, Iraqi Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf sent a letter to Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Wednesday charging that a number of Chilean air crew members who were leaving Iraq on June 5 carried boxes suspected of containing items barred from export.
According to an unofficial translation from the Arabic, the letter did not specify the contents of the boxes. But one source said they were alleged to be archaeological artifacts.

Al-Sahaf said UNSCOM officials refused to permit the boxes to be subjected to a joint inspection. An UNSCOM official in New York was later alleged to have told a member of Iraq's U.N. mission the helicopter complaint would not be brought to the Security Council if the boxes could be inspected only by UNSCOM officials at the U.N. centre in Baghdad.
UNSCOM's deputy chief, Charles Duelfer, told reporters: "We have never tried to cut any kind of a deal. ... What we wish to do is have the question resolved by U.N. people on the ground in Baghdad."
Council members said the issue should be resolved between UNSCOM and Iraq on the basis of international conventions on diplomatic immunity.
